nodes.question: Where is the implementation of anaerobic digestion technology for cover crops considered most feasible?
nodes.answer: It is most feasible at animal farms, where co-digestion with animal manure is possible.
nodes.paragraph: 2017). A poten- tial problem with the ensiling of cover crops is their relatively high moisture content at the time of har - vest, which may cause problems for the fermentation. Such problems may be combated by co-ensiling cover crops with straw (Feng et al. 2019). To avoid losses of straw before the harvesting of cover crops and limit the number of field operations, the most viable strat- egy is to harvest the straw at the time of harvest of the main crop and store it until the cover crops also have been harvested (Fontaine et al. 2020a). Cover crops and other agricultural residues are not commonly used as exclusive feedstock in biogas plants (Feng et al. 2020; Thamsiriroj et al. 2012; Xie 215 Nutr Cycl Agroecosyst (2025) 130:213 232 Vol. : (123456789) et al. 2011). Common practice is to co-digest with animal manure (Feng et al. 2020). The implementa- tion of technology for anaerobic digestion of cover crops is thus most feasible at animal farms, where co- digestion with animal manure is possible.

nodes.paragraph: A review of past and recent research was undertaken to identify ways of reducing energy-related costs and envi- ronmental impacts associated with the operation of farmmachinery and on-farm energy use. Indirect energy use (e.g., use of fossil fuels in manufacturing inputs such as animal feed or fertilizer) is brie y covered in this analysis, however, other on-farm energy uses such as for heating orventilation of buildings and other sources of GHG emis- sions (e.g., biogenic methane from ruminant livestock, nitrous oxide emissions arising from animal manure andnitrogen fertilizer use) are not discussed. The work re ects, primarily, an Australian perspective, but it draws from relevant evidence reported elsewhere. The highly mecha- nized Australian agricultural systems resemble large-holder (arable) enterprises found in other parts of the world, par-ticularly the USA, Canada, Brazil, and Argentina [ 64]. Hence, the analysis presented here is also relevant to those systems. Therefore, a key focus of this review was tocritically discuss energy use and emissions from direct fossil fuel combustion on farms to power farm machinery, speci cally tractors.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the primary focus of the study mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The study assesses the environmental impacts of biogas production at an organic dairy farm using two different biogas scenarios involving cover crops and cattle manure.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Cover crops offer a potential biogas feedstock, and to enable continuous operation of the biogas plant, ensiling can be used for biomass pres- ervation. The aim of the present study was to assess the environmental impacts of biogas production at an organic dairy farm for two modelled scenarios: (1) harvesting and ensiling of cover crops and cereal straw and co-digestion with cattle manure, or (2) mono-digestion of cattle manure and direct cover crop soil incorporation. The biogas scenarios were mod- elled in a consequential LCA in relation to a common baseline without anaerobic digestion, with cover crop soil incorporation and field application of raw cattle manure. Biogas scenarios resulted in decreased global warming impacts of (1) 250 and (2) 120 Mg CO2eq for a 1000-hectare example dairy farm due to substi- tution of natural gas. However, emissions from ensil- ing, biogas plant operation, and agronomic effects increased other environmental impacts. nodes.answer: Ensiling is the technology commonly used for the preservation of animal feed and could also be applied to preserve cover crop biomass for biogas production.
nodes.paragraph: Fertilization with digestate could thus increase the share of directly plant-available N, which can be field applied at the right time to meet crop demand (Fon- taine et al. 2020a, b; M ller & M ller 2012). This could increase the N uptake efficiency, contributing to improved yields and lower losses of N to the envi- ronment (DCE 2021; Fr seth et al. 2014). Harvesting of cover crops could also lead to avoided emissions from their decomposition in the field, such as ammo- nia and nitrous oxide (Fr seth et al. 2014; Nadeem et al. 2012), and leaching of nitrate, which can take place when nitrate is released at times of low crop demand (DCE 2021). The harvesting and later appli- cation of digestate could thus result in more efficient nutrient use by the crops and lower emissions to the environment. nodes.question: What was the main focus of the case study conducted in the present study?
nodes.answer: The case study focused on the environmental impacts of biogas production at organic dairy farms, particularly the co-digestion of cattle manure with silage of cover crops and straw.
nodes.paragraph: Due to the widespread use of cover crops, including legumes, in organic farming, an organic dairy farm was chosen for a case study in the present study. Aside from the clear benefits with increased biogas production, the use of energy crops in biogas production may also have adverse effects related to changes in land use and soil carbon storage, as well as increased energy inputs for harvesting, transport and processing (Hamelin et al. 2014). These effects vary depending on the feedstock and case-specific factors (Hamelin et al. 2014; Hijazi et al. 2016) and the overall environmental consequences of such com- bined effects are insufficiently understood in the case of cover crop harvesting and co-digestion. Therefore, it is essential to assess the total environmental impact of the system to ensure that the use of cover crop in anaerobic digestion leads to reduced environmental impacts, for which life cycle assessment (LCA) is a suitable method. The objective of this study was to provide a com- prehensive assessment of the environmental impacts of biogas production at organic dairy farms, focus- ing on the co-digestion of cattle manure with silage of cover crops and straw.

nodes.question: What is the significance of agriculture, including livestock, in global anthropogenic GHG emissions?
nodes.answer: Agriculture, including livestock, is the third most important sector contributing to global anthropogenic GHG emissions after energy and industry sectors. In 2,010 estimated livestock emissions amounted to 8.1 GT CO2-eq, with the largest share coming from enteric methane.

nodes.question: Why is the environmental impact of beef cattle production significant?
nodes.answer: The environmental impact of beef cattle production is significant due to the emission of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Each cow releases an estimated quantity of methane annually, ranging from 154 to 264 pounds, contributing to a total of 231 billion pounds of methane released annually by the 1.5 billion cattle globally reared for meat production.

nodes.question: How do the emissions from agricultural production in the beef sector primarily manifest?
nodes.answer: The emissions from agricultural production in the beef sector primarily manifest as methane and nitrous oxide released during enteric fermentation and the management of animal waste.

nodes.question: How much methane gas can one sheep generate in a day, and what percentage of methane gases in New Zealand are contributed by sheep farming?
nodes.answer: One sheep can generate about 30 L of methane every day. In New Zealand, sheep farming contributes to 90% of the methane gases generated in the country.

nodes.paragraph: Abstract Purpose Agri-food systems across the globe are faced with the challenge of reducing their supply-chain emissions of green - house gases (GHGs) such as nitrous oxide (N2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), and methane (CH4). For instance, 10% of the UK S GHG emissions are generated by agriculture, and ~ 56% of these are generated by livestock production. Numerous mitigation measures are being proposed to reduce GHG emissions from ruminants (representing 70 to 80% of total livestock emissions), particularly from beef cattle (presenting 30 40% of total livestock emissions). Methods To explore such potential, first, a business-as-usual (BAU) partial cradle-to-finishing farmgate scale modelling framework was developed. The BAU systems (i.e. steady-state productivity based on primary data from the North Wyke Farm Platform) were built using ensemble modelling wherein the RothC process-based soil organic carbon (SOC) model was integrated into the life cycle assessment (LCA) framework to conduct a trade-off analysis related to mitigation measures applicable to the study system. Potential mitigation measures were applied to the BAU scenario.

nodes.paragraph: The interventions assessed included: (i) extensification; (ii) adopting anaerobic digestion technology; and (iii) the use of the nitrification inhibitor DCD and substitution of fertiliser nitrogen with symbiotically fixed nitrogen from legumes. Results The partial carbon footprint for 1 kg of beef liveweight gain leaving the farmgate could be reduced by 7.5%, 12%, or 26% by adopting nitrification inhibitors, white clover introduction (pending establishment success), and anaerobic digestion for manure management, respectively. Conclusions The findings highlight the importance of including emissions beyond the farmgate level to analyse the carbon footprint of different management scenarios in order to assess the sustainability of agri-food production systems.
